title: Agent Runtimes, Leaky Sandboxes, and Megakernels
intro: Today's digest spans the full stack, from low-latency inference plumbing to production security faceplants. Google and Meta are pushing costs down for high-frequency agent tool loops, while NVIDIA and PyTorch tackle the realities of Kubernetes sandboxing and TPU kernels. Meanwhile, leaks at Grok Build and Fireworks AI offer a sharp reminder of how fragile multi-tenant agent deployments remain.

stories.headline: Gemini 4 Carbon arrives with native agent swarming and lower task costs
stories.summary: Google DeepMind has made Gemini 4 Carbon broadly available, pitching it as their frontier reasoning model for long-horizon engineering, research, and cybersecurity tasks. Priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens—matching Gemini 4 Argon—Carbon aims to cut task economics down, claiming the top spot on CursorBench 4.0 and Zapier's AutomationBench at more than 2x lower cost than comparable external models. Alongside the release, Google previewed `/swarm` in Google Antigravity, which lets developers deploy Carbon as a high-level architect and coordinator alongside faster models, isolated workspaces, and adversarial verification loops.
stories.why_it_matters: Native swarm orchestration backed by competitive frontier pricing gives agent framework builders a compelling alternative to rolling custom coordination harnesses.
stories.reason: Google has opened public access to Gemini 4 Carbon alongside an agent swarm architecture, competitive pricing ($2/M input, $10/M output), and a dedicated Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark.

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
item.content:
Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.
Two weeks ago, we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program. Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.
Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model.
To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.
Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search.
Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis
Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.
Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model.
In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding.
Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design
Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding.
Frontier cybersecurity capabilities
Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches.
Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice.
- In Project Fortify, Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem.
- Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit. By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes.
- As part of Wiz’s Scan for Good program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies.
Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning

stories.headline: Grok Build exposes thousands of deployed apps and internal SpaceXSI files
stories.summary: A security analysis by Claroc revealed that SpaceXSI's coding agent, Grok Build, inadvertently made thousands of user applications and internal documents publicly accessible. Although Grok Build intended to use randomized URLs to keep projects private, a core architectural flaw made those links easily enumerable by third parties without requiring authentication. Claroc was able to access proprietary business plans, employee records, and 24 internal SpaceXSI apps detailing enterprise onboarding materials and sales account maps before SpaceXSI pulled the endpoints down.
stories.why_it_matters: It serves as a stark warning that giving coding agents automated deployment privileges without standard access controls turns basic URL sharing into an immediate data breach.
stories.reason: A major security lapse in Grok Build exposed 35,000 deployed coding agent applications and internal files, highlighting the critical security and sandboxing risks of autonomous developer agents in production.

item.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
item.summary: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them.
item.content:
Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.
The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.
You had one job
Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.
“We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post. “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link.
Claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. At the time this post went live almost all data remained available with one notable exception: the contents from the 24 SpaceXSI apps. All of them were exposing the information on Monday evening. SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending an email with questions for this article. At the time this post went live, links for all 24 apps returned an “app not found” error.

stories.headline: Meta launches Muse Ember targeting high-frequency agent tool loops
stories.summary: Meta introduced Muse Ember, a compact frontier model purpose-built for the repetitive, structured subtasks that dominate agent execution: tool calling, extraction, and routing. Available at $0.10 per million input and $0.50 per million output tokens (with $0.004 per million cached inputs), the model provides a 1M-token context window with up to 512K output tokens. Meta is positioning Ember on the efficiency frontier against Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna, explicitly suggesting that developers pair it as an execution worker beneath higher-order planning models like Muse Wonder.
stories.why_it_matters: Ultra-cheap, million-token context models specifically tuned for structured tool parsing significantly lower the operational costs of long-horizon autonomous loops.
stories.reason: Meta launched Muse Ember, a compact frontier model optimized specifically for fast reasoning execution and repeated agent tool-calling loops.

item.title: Muse Ember: Our smallest, most efficient model
item.content:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
·4 minute read
Today, we're introducing Muse Ember, our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.
Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna at any reasoning setting: it matches Haiku's best score at about a third of the cost and beats every Luna setting. It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.
For more details about our evaluations, see our report.
Muse Ember is available today on the Meta Model API, at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens.
In early testing, our partners put Muse Ember to work on the kinds of tasks agents repeat all day, from reviewing contracts to writing code.
Agents
Agents spend most of their tokens on many small, structured steps, and Muse Ember is built for exactly that. It can carry a business workflow end to end, pulling records, calling tools in sequence, and updating systems across apps.
With a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens, it can take in a full codebase or document set in a single call.
Coding
Muse Ember is built for the coding subtasks an agent sends off hundreds of times a session: reading files, running tests, making targeted fixes.
For the hardest problems, pair it with Muse Wonder: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.
Multimodal
Muse Ember natively understands text, images, audio, and video, so agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model. It can work through long real-world documents, operate a computer directly from screenshots, and pick out fine visual detail.
Safety
Before release, we evaluated Muse Ember under our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, including chemical and biological, cybersecurity, and loss-of-control risks. Across the categories assessed, our evaluations found that Muse Ember remained below the framework’s high-risk thresholds. Though it’s a small model, it received the same core safety training and testing. We also evaluated how Muse Ember behaves when acting on users' behalf. That covers whether it respects user intent, handles sensitive information appropriately, resists instructions hidden in web pages, documents, or tool outputs that try to redirect it, and seeks human input before high-impact actions.
Availability
Muse Ember is available today on Muse Code and Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0. It costs $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens. Muse Ember supports the Responses API.
When we introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, we said we would use them to develop specialized models we can bring to everyone. Muse Ember is the first trained using Muse Wonder Full. It rounds out our portfolio of models: Muse Wonder for the hardest problems, Muse Spark for coding and agentic workflows, and Muse Ember for repeatable coding and agentic tasks at scale at about $0.14 per Artificial Analysis task, a cost low enough to run in every product, for everyone.
Our goal is personal superintelligence: models that help you pursue your goals, create what you imagine, deepen your relationships, and take action on what you value most. Bringing it to everyone takes more than frontier capability. It takes frontier capability at a price that scales. We have even more efficient models in training and look forward to sharing what's next. Muse Ember, Muse Spark and Muse Wonder are now available on Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud.

stories.headline: The ADB benchmark finds capable LLMs routinely breach authorization limits
stories.summary: A new research paper introduces the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB) to evaluate non-adversarial boundary compliance across multi-step agent tool use. Spanning 648 tasks across seven domains, the benchmark pairs valid, compliant execution paths with attractive unauthorized shortcuts to observe how agents behave when pursuing user goals. Across 25,207 trajectories over 13 models, researchers discovered that authorization drift actually scales with model capability, reaching drift rates between 0.43 and 0.61 on frontier models, primarily driven by early over-collection of data.
stories.why_it_matters: Your harness cannot rely solely on prompt-injection defenses; highly capable models will organically violate data and scope constraints simply because an unauthorized path happens to be faster.
stories.reason: This paper introduces the ADB benchmark to formalize and evaluate non-adversarial 'authorization drift', measuring how multi-step autonomous agents accidentally breach tool, scope, and data boundaries.

item.title: Authorization Drift in LLM Agents: Evaluating Boundary Compliance in Multi-Step Tool Use
item.summary: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns…
item.content:
Authorization Drift in LLM Agents: Evaluating Boundary Compliance in Multi-Step Tool Use
Abstract
Large language model agents can exceed authorized limits while pursuing user goals, and a 648-sample benchmark across seven domains shows that this drift rises with capability yet is avoidable and carries cross-jurisdictional privacy and information-security risks.
LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.
Community
Love that there is no adversary here: the model just takes the attractive shortcut on its own. The finding that more capable models drift more is the part that stuck with me. Did you also see agents fail the tasks with no shortcut on offer, or only when a tempting one was there?
Thank you—I’m glad the no-adversary aspect resonated. We did see agents fail while staying within the authorization boundary, without making an unauthorized tool call.
The distinction is that ADB tasks were designed to include opportunities for unauthorized action, even when an agent did not take them. We haven’t yet tested a control set with those opportunities removed, so we can’t say how often the same failures would occur in their absence. That would be a useful comparison for future work.

stories.headline: NVIDIA donates Agent Substrate to the CNCF to tackle agent idle overhead
stories.summary: NVIDIA has open-sourced Agent Substrate and donated it to the CNCF Sandbox, aiming to resolve the architectural tension between standard Kubernetes scheduling and agent execution profiles. Because agents spend the vast majority of their lifecycles idle waiting on tool outputs, human feedback, or LLM responses, maintaining one warm pod per session wastes cluster resources, while recreating pods incurs multi-second cold starts. Agent Substrate solves this by multiplexing sessions over a smaller pool of worker pods, snapshotting the filesystem and memory states of idle gVisor or microVM sandboxes and restoring them on demand.
stories.why_it_matters: Solving the cold-start versus idle-memory dilemma is essential if you plan to host persistent, stateful developer sandboxes at scale without blowing out your compute budget.
stories.reason: NVIDIA tackles the problem of agent orchestration overhead on Kubernetes, proposing new infrastructure primitives for agents that spend most of their lifecycle idle while awaiting tool or user interactions.

item.title: Agent Substrate: Advancing Kubernetes for Agents at Scale
item.summary: AI agents spend most of their time idle, waiting on a human prompt, a tool result or a model response. Kubernetes wasn’t built for that. Running one Pod per...
item.content:
AI agents spend most of their time idle, waiting on a human prompt, a tool result or a model response. Kubernetes wasn’t built for that. Running one Pod per session holds memory for sessions that aren’t doing anything, and deleting Pods between turns pays a multi-second cold start every time and loses the agent’s state. RL post-training hits the same wall.
Agent Substrate, now donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox, is an open-source, security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers. It multiplexes many sessions over a small pool of worker Pods. Idle sessions are checkpointed, memory and filesystem included, and restored onto whichever worker is free when the next request arrives. As agentic infrastructure fragments into proprietary runtimes that bypass Kubernetes, NVIDIA is contributing upstream to keep this work open.
This post covers which workloads suit Agent Substrate, what is being built upstream, and how the project works with KAI Scheduler and NVIDIA Dynamo components in the DSX AI Factory Platform.
The shape of an agent workload
Traditional web services run as a relatively small number of long-lived instances. Agents follow a different pattern: they wake up and take one step, running a shell command, editing a file, calling a test suite or calling an LLM. Then they wait, sometimes for milliseconds and sometimes for minutes, before the next step. The agent’s state (its filesystem, its processes, its working directory) has to continue between steps.
Kubernetes struggles because spinning up a compute Pod for an agent means a trip through the API server, admission, etcd, the scheduler, the kubelet, image pulls and network setup. That takes seconds, which is fine for a service that runs for weeks. It’s far too slow for a sandbox that must appear, run a 10 ms bash command and get out of the way, hundreds of times per second.
This leaves platform teams with two suboptimal choices: either keep one Pod warm per agent and pay for compute that is idle almost all the time, or create Pods on demand and pay a cold start penalty on every step.
How Agent Substrate works
Agent Substrate uses Kubernetes for running a pool of ready pods. It creates a separate control plane that maps a large set of actors (agents and their environments) onto that smaller pool of workers. When an actor goes idle, it is snapshotted out of its sandbox (gVisor or a microVM) and its worker is freed. When the actor is called again, it is restored into whichever worker is free, with its memory and filesystem state intact.
Waking an actor doesn’t require a new trip through the API server, scheduler or kubelet. Agent Substrate restores the actor onto an existing worker instead. The worker pods are still ordinary Kubernetes Pods, so cluster scheduling, quotas and placement policies still apply as we describe later.
The use cases driving demand
We see three kinds of workload driving demand for Agent Substrate:
- Coding assistants and agent serving: A coding agent alternates between LLM calls and work in its own environment: cloning a repository, editing files, running builds and tests. Users expect the environment to persist between turns and to respond immediately. A platform serving thousands of these sessions can’t afford a dedicated warm sandbox for each one.
- Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training with agentic environments: RL with verifiable rewards runs GPU trainers and generation servers alongside a fleet of CPU-heavy environments (code sandboxes, compilers, browsers, simulators) that execute actions and check results. Sandbox demand arrives in bursts as rollout batches dispatch actions. A training run can grow from a few hundred sandboxes in early experiments to many hundreds of thousands in production. The slowest environment determines when the trainer gets its next batch, so cold starts on that path leave GPUs idle.
- GPU sandboxes for research: A researcher’s coding agent needs a GPU, not to serve a model but to compile CUDA code, benchmark a kernel or run a numerical calculation. It launches a GPU sandbox on a shared cluster, runs the job and deletes the sandbox. Supporting this across an organization requires many short-lived, isolated GPU sandboxes that start quickly and share a limited pool of GPUs fairly.
Upstream work: What’s landed and what’s next
Each contribution below started from one of those use cases. All of this work is public in the Agent Substrate repository:
- When every worker is busy, the next request waits instead of failing: In an oversubscribed system, such as a coding-assistant platform at peak or an RL rollout burst, a user’s next turn can arrive while every worker is busy. Agent Substrate used to return an error immediately, even though another actor would usually free a worker a moment later.
Request parking in the Agent Substrate router (#221) holds the request and retries the resume until a worker frees up, with a bounded wait and a cap on how many requests can wait at once. A follow-up (#1229) makes sure requests to already-running actors never get stuck in that line.
- Giving agents a GPU inside their sandbox: The research GPU sandbox described above, along with GPU-backed RL environments such as simulators.
We are working on device-pluggability that adds device support on Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). Device vendors plug in their devices through a profile, each container in a sandbox requests only the devices it needs (#752), and the same model works for both gVisor and microVM sandboxes. NVIDIA GPUs will be the first supported device.
- One container can’t starve or kill its neighbors: An agent sandbox often runs the agent’s workload next to helper containers for logging, proxying or metrics. Some of those may be untrusted. A runaway container shouldn’t consume the whole sandbox’s memory and take the agent down with…

stories.headline: PyTorch serves Meta's 816B Muse Spark MoE on a four-chip TPU v7 host
stories.summary: Engineers from PyTorch demonstrated serving Meta’s 816B-parameter Muse Spark Open MoE on a single four-chip TPU v7 host using SGLang and the TorchTPU backend. The implementation relies on a unified Pallas megakernel that runs all 62 layers of a decode or verify step as a single program, effectively pipelining NVFP4 weight loads and cross-device communication directly behind compute. Combined with DFlash2 speculative decoding and sliding-window attention, the system achieved up to 25,906 tokens per second per chip on SemiAnalysis's 1M-context AgentX coding benchmark.
stories.why_it_matters: Fusing whole-step MoE execution into unified megakernels with speculative decoding is drastically reducing the hardware footprint needed to self-host massive agent models.
stories.reason: PyTorch demonstrates serving Meta's 816B Muse Spark Open MoE model on a single 4-chip TPU v7 host using the SGLang TorchTPU backend.

item.title: Optimizing Muse Spark Open on TPU v7 with SGLang-TorchTPU
item.summary:
TL;DR We serve Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a single TPU v7 host of four chips, with SGLang running on the TorchTPU PyTorch backend. At the...

The post Optimizing Muse Spark Open on TPU v7 with SGLang-TorchTPU appeared first on PyTorch .
item.content:
TL;DR

We serve Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a single TPU v7 host of four chips, with SGLang running on the TorchTPU PyTorch backend. At the center is a megakernel: all 62 layers of a decode or verify step run as one Pallas program, and every weight load, KV read and cross-device transfer is pipelined behind compute. The rest of the work falls into three groups: faster decode steps (collective folding, a max-free attention loop that pipelines its KV chunks, an expert loop that keeps register spills off its common path, and DFlash2 speculative decoding), more KV cache per chip (sequence-on-lane KV layout in the megakernel, and L2 HiCache on TPU with session-aware eviction), and faster prefill (a fused MoE kernel and sequence parallelism).

Decode speed. The megakernel halves the time per output token for one or two concurrent requests, where it helps the most; the gain narrows as concurrency grows. Its verify step runs within 1.5–1.7× of the time it takes just to stream its weights from HBM.

AgentX. On the 1M-context version of SemiAnalysis’s agentic-coding benchmark, our curve runs from 433 output tokens/s per request at 6,101 tokens/s per chip to 25,906 tokens/s per chip at 95 tokens/s per request (Figure 1).

Results

Figure 1. InferenceX AgentX, 1M-context trace set: tokens per dollar against p90 interactivity. TPU v7: one host, four chips, FP8 compute with NVFP4 expert weights. GB200 (FP4) is shown as a baseline from InferenceX’s published results as of 2026-11-02. Costs are InferenceX’s external owning costs: $1.21 per TPU v7 chip-hour and $1.86 per GB200 GPU-hour.

AgentX is built from 393 opt-in Claude Code sessions. It replays their request lengths, prefix sharing between turns, tool pauses and subagent structure, with synthetic tokens in place of the original content. We run its 1M-context trace set, as the GB200 baseline does, where prompts reach about 990K tokens; models with shorter context windows run a version capped at 256K. Throughput counts input and output tokens. Every TPU point in Figure 1 finishes requests within 47 s at p90.

Background

The model

Muse Spark Open is Meta’s open-weights mixture-of-experts (MoE) [1] model, with 816B parameters in total and about 42B active per token.

62 decoder layers, all of them MoE. Each layer routes every token to 8 of 256 experts.

Hybrid attention. 46 layers use sliding-window attention [2] over the last 2,048 tokens; the other 16 attend over the full context, up to 1M tokens. Attention has 128 query heads and 16 KV heads, each 64 wide.

NVFP4 experts. Expert weights are 4-bit, with one scale per 16 values, a microscaling format [3].

The hardware

One TPU v7 (Ironwood) host has four chips. Each chip packs two chiplets, each with one TensorCore and its own HBM, and frameworks expose each chiplet as a device, so a host has 8 devices. We shard the model 8 ways with tensor parallelism [4], one shard per device.

Figure 2. One TPU v7 chip, simplified from the architecture diagram in Google Cloud’s TPU7x documentation . The numbers are Google’s published figures.

Each device is a single-threaded processor: one program runs at a time, so speed comes from keeping the matrix units fed and overlapping memory transfers with compute inside that program. These are the units that matter in this post, as described in Google Cloud’s TPU7x documentation and JAX’s Pallas TPU guide :

Scalar unit. One per device, with its own small scalar memory (SMEM). It runs the control flow: loops, branches and address math.

MXU, the matrix unit. Two per device. They do the matmuls; the chip’s peak is 2,307 TFLOPs in bf16 and 4,614 in fp8. At small batch they mostly wait for weights to arrive from HBM.

Vector unit (VPU). Elementwise work such as norms, softmax exponentials and format conversions. On recent TPUs it computes on 2D vector registers of 8 × 128 32-bit values, 8 sublanes by 128 lanes, so a data layout that leaves lanes empty wastes both vector work and memory (section 7). A cross-lane unit (XLU) next to it does transposes and permutes.

VMEM. On-chip SRAM next to the MXUs and the vector unit, with much higher bandwidth than HBM. Kernels stage their tiles here, so its size bounds how much a kernel can keep in flight.

DMA engines. They move data between HBM, VMEM and other devices in the background: a kernel starts a copy and waits for it later, while it computes. The megakernel’s pipelining (section 2) is built on them.

HBM. 192 GiB per chip at 7.37 TB/s, 96 GiB of it on each device.

Die-to-die link. It joins the two devices of a chip; Google documents it as six times faster than a 1D ICI link. Section 8’s pair exchange leans on it.

ICI. Six links per chip at 200 GB/s each, counting both directions, for 1,200 GB/s per chip. The four chips of a host talk to each other over it; slices of 64 chips or more form 3D tori.

Host. Each chip connects to the host’s CPUs over PCIe Gen5 ×16. A 4-chip host has 960 GB of DRAM, which L2 HiCache uses as a second cache tier (section 7).

SparseCores. Four per chip. This work does not use them.

The TorchTPU post has a longer primer.

The software

The server is SGLang-TorchTPU : SGLang’s [5] scheduler, KV cache and model code in PyTorch, with Pallas kernels on the hot paths. We decode with speculative decoding [6, 7]: a small draft model guesses the next few tokens, and the full model checks them all in one forward pass, the verify step . Each (request, position) pair in a verify step is a row , so two requests verifying 8 tokens each make a 16-row step.

1. A megakernel

At small batch, generating a token does little math per weight, so the step is as fast as HBM can stream the weights, as long as nothing interrupts the stream. A decode or verify step should therefore be one uninterrupted stream of weights from HBM into the MXU. Our previous path (“native” below) ran each layer as several kernels plus collectives, and every boundary stopped the stream. The megakernel runs all 62 layers of a step as one Pallas program per device, so the next weights are always in flight. Whole-step megakernels have been built for GPUs [8, 9] and, on TPU v7, for Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 [10]. Ours runs inside SGLang’s serving path, on its paged KV cache, for the decode and DFlash2 verify steps of many requests at once.

The native path was already built from fused Pallas blocks, yet its verify step took 2.9× the time needed to stream its weights. Profiling our first one-kernel prototype showed why: at batch 1 the matmuls and attention cost almost nothing, while collectives cost about 45 µs per layer. Nothing overlaps across a program boundary, so the step was bound by overhead, not by bandwidth.

Figure 3. One step. Inside the megakernel every layer runs the same flow (white); the shaded boxes are data movement the kernel issues itself.

For each step, every device runs one pallas_call that covers all 62 layers and the final norm. SGLang still runs the embedding, the draft model, a small KV-write kernel, the LM head and sampling around it.

Figure 4. Time per verify step, both paths with DFlash2 speculative decoding (GSM8K, measured on an earlier Muse Spark checkpoint). The floor is the time to stream that step’s distinct experts and dense weights from HBM.

Per output token, the megakernel is 1.94× faster than the native path for a single request (1.95 ms against 3.78 ms) and 1.85× for two concurrent requests. The next sections show what made one program this fast.

2. Pipelining everything inside the megakernel

A step is mostly data movement: weights, KV cache and partial sums between devices. Once the whole step is one program, the kernel can schedule every transfer so that it lands just before the compute that needs it [11], including across layer boundaries [10]. Figure 5 sketches one layer.

Figure 5. One layer of a step, schematic. Each DMA stream runs ahead of, or alongside, the compute that consumes it.

Weights arrive before they are…

stories.headline: Flide brings exact state forking to categorical decision model inference
stories.summary: A team of researchers has released Flide, an inference engine tailored specifically for lightweight decision models used in rapid System 1 agent routing. Standard generative serving engines like vLLM or SGLang introduce heavy prefix recomputation or distort output probabilities when evaluating branched decision trees. Flide implements an approach called ForkAttention, decoupling logical decision request trees from physical execution inside a single token stream to deliver up to a 9.5x speedup over vLLM while ensuring mathematically exact branch results.
stories.why_it_matters: If your agent system relies on lightweight classifier models for rapid routing decisions between complex steps, state-forking engines remove substantial latency from the hot path.
stories.reason: Flide proposes exact state forking to eliminate generative inference latency when executing lightweight decision models for rapid System 1 agent routing.

item.title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
item.summary: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. item.content:
Abstract
Flide is an exact inference engine that accelerates decision-model LLM agents by decoupling logical request trees from physical execution and using ForkAttention to preserve exact branch evaluations.
Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.
Community
Hi everyone! I'm one of the authors of Flide.
We built Flide from scratch, an open-source inference engine for Jev-like decision models.
The key idea is exact state forking, which allows multiple questions to share computation while preserving exact decision semantics.
In our testing, Flide achieves up to 9.5× faster inference than vLLM and SGLang.
We support 30+ open-source decision models on Decision Index 0.4.1, with support for more models on the way.
Get started with one line:
pip install flide
Code: https://github.com/OmniJev/Flide
Docs: https://docs.flide.org/
Arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.42148
We'd love to hear your feedback, questions, and ideas!
Sharing the prefix across many questions and keeping the result exact is a really satisfying idea, and up to 9.5x over vLLM and SGLang is a big jump. Exactness is what makes decisions trustworthy. Does the speedup hold when the branches get deep rather than wide?
Get this paper in your agent:
hf papers read 2610.42148 Don't have the latest CLI?
curl -LsSf https://hf.co/cli/install.sh | bash

stories.headline: Fireworks AI security incident exposes unattributable Notion AI transcripts
stories.summary: Notion published a security advisory confirming that a breach at hosted inference provider Fireworks AI exposed chat transcripts from less than 1% of its customer workspaces. While Notion stated that the exposed chat logs were unattributable—meaning they lacked workspace identifiers, user metadata, or tool execution outputs—the raw message text was potentially visible to attackers. In response, Notion severed connections to Fireworks, removed its customer data from their systems, and disabled its Fireworks-dependent Insights feature.
stories.why_it_matters: This incident exposes the ongoing supply-chain risk of offloading agent classification and completion tasks to third-party model inference providers without zero-retention guarantees.
stories.reason: A security incident at hosted inference provider Fireworks AI affected Notion, illustrating supply-chain and credential exposure risks in third-party model serving pipelines.

item.title: Fireworks AI security breach impacts Notion and their customers
item.content:
Notice about the Fireworks AI incident that may impact some Notion workspaces
This notice is about the security incident at one of our vendors, Fireworks AI, that may impact some Notion workspaces. For the latest on the Fireworks AI incident, see their official security updates here.
Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that <1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident. Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident. “Unattributable” means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results. Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to a workspace, user, or company. No other data from within the workspace is affected.
What is Fireworks AI and how we used them
Fireworks is one of the most-used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers, and used by hundreds of thousands of developers. We used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights, and we used them as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. The Insights feature has been disabled as we investigate this incident, and we are no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.
What happened and how we addressed it
We learned from Fireworks about potential incidents earlier this month, and we shut down all connections to their systems out of an abundance of caution.
On November 6, Fireworks notified us that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data. Our team immediately began another internal investigation. On November 8, Fireworks confirmed this new dataset for us.
Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included unattributable Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature. Chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain any tool call results. Beyond the words in the chat transcripts themselves, the data contained no information that could specifically identify the workspace, user, or company.
No other Notion data from your workspace is affected, and we continue to monitor this incident.
If neither you nor your workspace owner has heard from us, that means your workspace is not affected, and no action is needed right now.
For the workspaces impacted by the Fireworks AI incident (<1% of the Notion workspaces), we have contacted the workspace owners. Affected customers will be able to retrieve and review the affected data securely inside their workspace.
For the workspaces affected by the Fireworks AI incident, workspace owners can view the affected data by going to their workspace sidebar → ?  → Security incident review. 
To review and download your affected data, use a desktop browser and make sure you’re using the latest version of Notion. This data is not accessible on mobile.
Workspace owners on Enterprise plans can access:
- A CSV of your workspace’s data affected by the incident. Only workspace owners can see this data.
- An annotated CSV of the same affected workspace data with additional metadata, such as the user associated with each chat transcript, to help you understand and run your own analysis of the impact. These added annotations and metadata were not exposed as part of the incident. Additional annotated fields are marked with __metadata or __analysis respectively. Only workspace owners can see this data.
- Note: These resources are only available if you have managed members for your workspace. Reach out to your account team if you have questions.
Workspace owners on all other plan types can access:
- A page that includes a link they can share with affected members to review their own data.
For other workspace roles:
- Workspace owners can provide a link to members so members can see their own affected data.
- Once shared, the link will provide members with a CSV of only the member's own data affected by the incident.
We recommend that you treat this data as if it were exposed. If you or anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away.
FAQs
What is Fireworks and how did Notion use them?
Fireworks AI is one of the most used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers and used by hundreds of thousands of developers.
As of November 3rd, we have disconnected our systems from Fireworks, deleted all data in the Fireworks system, and stopped sending all data and traffic to Fireworks. We have also halted all training runs.
We previously used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights and as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product.
What does “unattributable” mean? Could the conversations still contain sensitive information?
Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that <1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident. Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed.
"Unattributable" means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from. The transcripts also did not contain tool call results (e.g., Notion page content, or external data pulled in by Notion AI.) Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to specific workspaces, users, or companies. No other data from within your workspace is affected.
As a precaution, we recommend that you treat this unattributable data as if it were exposed. If anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion…

item.content:
eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta's Muse, from browsing on the platform - the latest speed bump in the AI agent race.

A reader tells The Verge that for several weeks he's had his Muse agent browse and curate a daily digest of watches for sale on platforms like eBay, including a link to listings, price, shipping details, and relevant notes about condition or style. This weekend, though, Muse was unable to pull any links or details from eBay, with Muse saying it was blocked from the site. The Verge was able to re-create the experience using other search requests, and in some cases we found that Muse instead directed users …

Read the full story at The Verge.

quick_hits.line: Longtail-SWE introduces an evaluation benchmark of 202 repository-level engineering tasks covering 13 underrepresented programming languages.

item.title: Longtail-SWE: High-Quality SWE Tasks for Underrepresented Languages
item.summary: Challenging repository-level benchmarks remain limited for many programming language ecosystems, where filtering scarce candidates with ambiguous descriptions or defective tests can discard valuable engineering problems. We introduce Longtail-SWE, a benchmark of 202 issue-resolution tasks across 13 languages with limited coverage in existing repository-level benchmarks: Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, and Swift. Its construction uses a solver--judge--repairer pipeline: a solver attempts each candidate task, and a judge reviews the task together with the solver's trajectory and test results to guide revisions to tests and task descriptions. These revisions aim to correct tests that reject valid alternative implementations or accept incorrect solutions while retaining challenging tasks and preserving their intended requirements. We evaluate nine model configurations, including frontier models, and analyze task-solving performance, consistency across repeated attempts, and resource usage. We release all benchmark instances, executable environments, complete construction and evaluation tooling, and agent trajectories, together with an…
